target_customer: Presenters and small teams who need to show their screen to remote viewers without asking them to install software, plus developers who embed screen sharing through an API
problem: Sharing a screen with someone outside the company usually required downloads, accounts or paid conferencing tools. Screenleap let a presenter start a share in one click and let viewers join in a browser on any device.
business_model: Freemium SaaS with paid tiers for presenters plus a screen sharing API for developers

founders.name: Lawrence Gentilello
previous_startups: Launched an early online Facebook at Stanford in 1999 (per YC page, outcome not stated)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as founder and board director and says he co-founded Screenleap. The co-founder is not named on any page I opened. His later company Optery (W22) is after this company.

competitors.name: Google+ Hangouts
competitors.what: Video hangouts that had just added screen sharing but required every participant to sign up and log in

competitors.name: WebEx
competitors.what: Paid web conferencing with call in numbers and richer sharing tools, suggested by the article for heavier needs

technical_complexity.rationale: Browser based viewing of a live desktop stream on any device without plugins was demanding in 2012 for a four person team, though the screen capture itself was a known problem. The company page still describes API and mobile apps, which adds scope.

defensibility.rationale: The pitch was convenience, and larger vendors such as Google could add the same no install viewing. No network effects or data advantage are documented.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Incumbents kept adding browser based sharing over time. No source I opened shows an acquisition or a copy aimed at Screenleap, and the company still operates as of the 2026 site fetch.

market_need_then: The March 2012 TNW launch coverage contrasted Screenleap with Hangouts, which forced sign ups, and WebEx, which cost money, so the pain was friction in ad hoc sharing with outsiders. No spend figures were found.

branding.domain_note: Uses screenleap.com. No purchase history found.

identity.logo: not described in any source I opened
identity.visual_style: plain product site focused on the share button
identity.voice_and_tone: functional and direct, headline reads Share your screen instantly to any device with a browser

branding.brand_signature: The Dropbox for screen sharing positioning statement on the YC page
branding.community_and_virality: Press mentions listed on the company site include TechCrunch, Mashable, CNET, Lifehacker and The Next Web. The site shows a Trustpilot rating of 4.5 from 445 reviews.

brand_strength.rationale: Early blog coverage helped launch, but no source shows a lasting brand asset or community, and the name is descriptive of function rather than distinctive.

outcome_analysis: Screenleap is still operating more than a decade after Winter 2012 with a small team, a screen sharing and meetings product and an API. No venture round is documented beyond the YC deal, and no exit is found. The picture is a steady small business in a space where Google, Cisco and Zoom later made browser based sharing a default feature, so growth looks capped rather than failed.
notes: Two outcome and funding searches returned nothing about an exit or shutdown. CB Insights snippet (aggregator, page itself returned 403) lists about 20 thousand dollars in 2012 from Y Combinator across two rounds. That figure is unverified and the YC standard deal is not recorded as a round. A comparison site claims the presenter needs Java, which Screenleap's own pages contradict; not used. The brand search found nothing about the name or logo.
